summary:
The k-th highest bid is the value at index `n − k` of the sorted bids. Quickselect finds it without sorting:
partition around a random pivot (three ways, so repeats are handled), then continue only in the part that
contains index `n − k`. Expected O(n).

question.md:
Return the k-th highest bid, counting repeats: in `[9, 9, 5]` the 2nd highest is 9.

- **Repeats count separately**, so this is "the value at sorted position k from the top".
- **Up to 10⁵ bids** and k anywhere from 1 to n.

**Edge cases to keep in mind**

- Repeats count separately: in `[9, 9, 5]` the 2nd highest is 9.
- `k = 1` is the maximum; `k = n` the minimum.
- The k-th highest is the value at sorted (ascending) index `n − k`.

think.md:
**Quickselect: quick sort that only follows one side.** To find the value at sorted position `t`, partition around a
pivot into `< p | = p | > p`. The `= p` block already sits at its final sorted positions `lt … gt`:

- if `t` falls inside `lt … gt`, the answer is the pivot;
- if `t < lt`, the answer is in the left part, so continue only there;
- if `t > gt`, continue only in the right part.

**Why it's O(n) on average.** A random pivot splits the range roughly in half on average, and only one half is kept:
`n + n/2 + n/4 + … ≈ 2n` comparisons. The worst case is O(n²) (consistently terrible pivots), which randomness makes
vanishingly unlikely. Three-way partitioning keeps repeated values from causing that worst case.
**Quickselect on `[12, 40, 7, 40, 25, 3, 18]` for the 3rd highest** (sorted index 4); the pivot is random, one possible run:

approaches.title: Min-heap of the k highest

idea.md:
Keep a min-heap of the `k` largest bids seen so far: push each bid, and pop the smallest whenever the heap
exceeds `k`. At the end the heap's minimum is the k-th highest.

build: Push each bid; pop when size exceeds `k`.

lines.text: A min-heap that will hold the k highest bids seen so far.
More than k kept: the smallest can't be among the k highest any more.

notes.c: Remove the root and sift the last value down.

lines.text: The smallest of the k highest is the k-th highest.

steps.text: Add 40; more than 3 kept, so drop the smallest, 7.
Add 25; more than 3 kept, so drop the smallest, 12.
Add 3; more than 3 kept, so drop the smallest, 3.
Add 18; more than 3 kept, so drop the smallest, 18.
The heap's smallest is the 3-th highest: 25.

walk.title: Keep a min-heap of the 3 highest bids seen so far; its top is the k-th highest.

approaches.title: Three-way quickselect

idea.md:
Quickselect for sorted index `n − k` with three-way partitioning and a random pivot, narrowing `lo … hi`
to the side that contains the target until it lands in the pivot block.

build: Keep the side containing the target.

lines.text: A copy to rearrange, and the target index: the k-th highest is at `n − k` in ascending order.
The answer is somewhere in `a[lo..hi]`; at first, the whole array.
Three-way partition around a random pivot value: `< p` to the front, `> p` to the back, copies of `p` in the middle.
After partitioning, `a[lt..gt]` holds exactly the pivot's copies, in their sorted positions. If the target index is among them, that's the answer; otherwise keep only the side that contains it.
Free the copy and return the value found.

complexity.md: **Time O(n)** expected, O(n²) worst case. **Space O(n)** for the copy (O(1) in place).

steps.text: We want the value that would sit at index 4 after sorting (n − k = 7 − 3).
Pivot 40: smaller values fill 0..4, copies of 40 fill 5..6. Index 4 is in the smaller part: keep only that part.
Pivot 25 fills 4..4, which includes index 4: the answer is 25.

walk.title: Quickselect: the k-th highest is the value at index n − k in ascending order. Partition, then keep only the side holding that index.

takeaways.md:
- **k-th largest/smallest:** quickselect (expected O(n)) or a size-k heap (O(n log k), good for streams).
- Translate "k-th highest" to the ascending index `n − k`.
- **Pitfall:** two-way partitioning with many equal values.
